bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.capacity: several tents
bivy.water: the lake, and snowmelt runnels feeding it
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, and the standard first night on the traverse — the first place with water and flat ground after Cache Col. Sites sit on the lip of a steep slope that drops thousands of feet toward the valley, so pitch back from the edge in wind. The col above holds snow well into July and there is no water at the col itself, so parties crossing late in the day carry water up or drop to this lake. Goats work the camp for salt; keep gear and urine spots away from tents. The national park boundary runs at Cache Col just above; camps from here south are commonly described as lying in the wilderness outside the park where no camping permit is required, but confirm the zone with the ranger station when you pick up your trailhead permit.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.capacity: several tents
bivy.water: the lakes; flowing water available even under snow cover
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the usual second night, in heather meadow among granite boulders below the Le Conte Glacier. It is a low point on the traverse and melts out later than its elevation suggests — a party in late June found nothing bare and pitched on snow with running water alongside. Sheltered relative to the passes on either side, but the basin is a cold sink. Check the zone for permits.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.capacity: at least three good sites; more on snow
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the last true alpine camp and the one most parties would not skip, looking straight across at the icefalls of Dome and Sinister. Dry dirt bivy platforms are usable by late June, earlier than the lower camps. It is an open basin with nothing to hide behind: one party sat out roughly twelve hours of rain and wind in tents here, so anchor well and pick a site with a boulder on the windward side. Check the zone for permits.

bivy.name: Cub Lake meadows / Itswoot Ridge
bivy.capacity: many parties; the meadows absorb a dozen or more groups on a holiday weekend
bivy.water: Cub Lake outlet and meadow streams
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the last night for parties exiting south to Downey Creek, in heather meadow below Itswoot Ridge. Melts out late — a late-June party found the lake still largely frozen, the basin barely opened up, and a marginal perch near 6,200 ft below the basin that they would not recommend sleeping on until more snow had gone. Popular enough that solitude is not the reason to stop here; proximity to the Bachelor Creek descent is. Check the zone for permits.

bivy.name: Thornton Pass benches
bivy.capacity: a few tents on separate benches
bivy.water: lingering snow patches only — no reliable stream at camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and effectively the only base for this route: flat rock-and-heather benches on the ridge crest just south of the pass. Parties take most of a day to reach it — around seven and a half hours of brush and cliff-band navigation from the trailhead — and then run the whole climb as an enormous out-and-back from here. It is a crest site, so wind is the trade for the flat ground. Water is the real constraint: fill at Thornton Creek low on the approach, because by late summer the snow patches near the benches can be gone. Summit day commonly ends after dark, and finding these benches again in the dark is the crux of the return; the published alternative is a cold night out on the talus, which is an outcome to plan against rather than a site.

bivy.name: Upper Despair Lake
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: NOT a documented camp — reports use it as a rest and water stop on the long traverse to the peak, and no established sites are described there. It is the last reliable water before the cliff band below the southeast face, and worth knowing about as an EMERGENCY stopping point if a party is benighted on the traverse rather than as a planned camp. Snow patches and steep chutes linger around the Despair Lakes into early summer.

bivy.name: Bachelor Flats / Bachelor Meadows
bivy.capacity: multiple tents in the clearing
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the standard first night after leaving maintained trail at the Bachelor Creek crossing. An informal but heavily used forest camp in a clearing — sheltered, buggy, and low. Most parties stop here because the unmaintained climbers' path above eats time and the day from the car is already long.

bivy.name: Cub Lake meadows
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp in heather meadow past Cub Pass, and the busiest ground on the approach — a summer weekend has been described with a dozen or more parties spread through these meadows and several more on Itswoot Ridge above. Comfortable and well watered, but it leaves the glacier travel and the col for the following day.

bivy.name: Chikamin-Dome col
bivy.capacity: a small tent or several bivy sacks; a four-person tent needs building out
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one most parties use for Gunsight — an established site on the col reached by roping up at Itswoot Pass and crossing the Dome Glacier. Room is genuinely tight: one party spent half an hour of earthwork levelling ground for a four-person tent. It is a col, so it funnels wind, but it is reported as the sheltered option compared with the open glacier either side. Everything here is melted, so carry fuel accordingly.

bivy.name: Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face
bivy.capacity: small — a snow dome and rock outcrop, a tent or two
bivy.notes: PLANNED advanced camp, about ninety minutes of descending traverse below the col and directly under Gunsight's west face. Parties move here to shorten summit day rather than day-climbing from the col. It is a glacier bench: rope up moving to and from it, site the tent clear of the fall line off the face, and expect a cold, fully exposed pitch.

bivy.name: Crater Creek Meadows bench
bivy.capacity: small — comfortable for a party of two
bivy.water: Crater Creek, about 200 ft below camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard staging point for the south face, on a heather bench above Crater Creek northwest of point 7001. Reached in roughly eight hours and eleven miles from the car, after the Jerry Glacier traverse and the drop into Crater Creek Basin. Parties choose it over Jerry Lakes specifically because it shortens the summit day onto the face. Terrain gives moderate wind shelter. Permit status is not confirmed for this basin — check the zone before you go.

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes basin
bivy.capacity: multiple parties across the basin
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, a grassy boulder-strewn bowl with several separate sites; the best of them sits by the small lake between the two large ones. Snow-free by mid-August. It is the more pleasant camp of the two and the obvious stop if you arrive late, but it leaves a longer traverse to the face on summit day. Open bowl, so afternoon wind. Fire-scarred forest on the approach into the basin. Check the zone for permits.

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes Peak south saddle
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp — on record only as an unplanned night out, sat through in a bivy sack and an emergency blanket with little wind protection and a cold, sleepless result. Worth knowing exists if a party is caught on the ridge between the lakes and the Crater Mountain saddle, and worth planning not to use.

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.capacity: a couple of bivy-scale sites
bivy.notes: PLANNED intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow
bivy.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.

bivy.name: 5,500 ft bivy below the slabs
bivy.capacity: about four people
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the most commonly used one on this side of the peak. Reached after the slide-alder section and a crossing of the creek, tucked just below the low-angle slabs with rock walls around it and running water on hand. Nothing above it is comfortable, and the slabs above lead straight onto the glacier in the morning.

bivy.name: 5,200 ft camp to the west
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the fallback if you run out of daylight in the brush below. Perfectly serviceable, but reports consistently say the extra three hundred feet up to the higher bivy is worth carrying, because summit day from here is long enough already.

bivy.name: Goode Glacier toe
bivy.capacity: limited — a small number of usable flat spots, not a big-party site
bivy.water: scarce near camp late season; fill at the last reliable stream below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp on the moraine and rubble between roughly 6,400 and 6,800 ft. Flat ground is genuinely limited and the good spots are specific rather than general — expect to hunt for them, and expect glacier noise all night. It is the highest planned camp and the one that makes the couloir a reasonable day, but the water problem is real by late summer.

bivy.name: West Tower ledge, upper mountain
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp. A narrow shelf on the north side of the crest between the West Tower and the main summit, where a solo climber spent a night wedged between rocks and still lost sleep to constant south wind. No water, no flat ground worth the name, and a serious place to be caught. It exists, and that is the only reason to know about it.

bivy.name: Colonnade Ridge
bivy.capacity: snow platforms — build what you need
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay, obtained in person; a separate paid climbing permit is required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the first reasonable stopping point once you leave the Wonderland Trail and start up toward the Puyallup Cleaver. It is a snow camp, so it depends entirely on coverage — in a dry year the ground here is bare and the site is much less pleasant. Parties who stop here accept a very long summit day in exchange for an easier first day off the trail.

bivy.name: Puyallup Cleaver high camp
bivy.capacity: a few tents on cut platforms
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit also required at this elevation and on the glaciers above
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the usual high camp for the route, on the cleaver at roughly this height before it is left at about 8,500 ft for the glacier traverse. Mixed snow and rock, wind-exposed on a west-facing rib with nothing upwind of it. Site on the cleaver crest rather than in a runnel, and keep clear of the loose rock edges.

bivy.name: Open bivouac near 9,600 ft
bivy.capacity: a bivy sack or two
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft
bivy.notes: PLANNED but committing — used specifically to cut the summit day down, and on record as an open bivouac rather than a sheltered site. There is nothing here but what you dig. In a dry season the transition from this height onto the face is the part that turns parties around, so the higher camp only pays off if the snow is in.

bivy.name: Bergschrund camp in the Sunset Amphitheater
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp reached by leaving the cleaver near 8,500 ft, traversing the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers and climbing a steep snow gully to a small bergschrund with good ground beside it. The caution is the amphitheater itself: the headwall above sheds ice and rock, so this only makes sense sited where the schrund and the terrain put you out of the fall line, and it is worth reaching it early and cold rather than in afternoon sun.

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp
bivy.capacity: a party of several
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, flat dry ground near Whatcom Pass at the end of the maintained trail and the last comfortable night of the trip — reports describe it as vastly more pleasant than anything above. This is where the route leaves trail for the Whatcom Glacier traverse, about four and a half hours and 1,750 ft of gain below Perfect Pass. Sheltered valley-head position. A knoll above the pass around 6,500 ft is also camped, with water a rock-hop away at the creek.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass
bivy.capacity: a few tents on slabs and heather
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, and widely rated one of the finest bivy sites in the range — granite slabs, reliable running water, and the Challenger Glacier starting at the doorstep. It is the standard last camp before roping up. Open and high, so weather arrives without warning; parties have had to navigate back down to it in fog off the glacier, which is an argument for marking it before you leave in the morning.

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier lateral moraine
bivy.capacity: tight — a narrow strip, enough for a small party
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the base for the climb itself, on the narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the glacier after crossing the high bench near 8,100 ft and dropping through the West Challenger notch. Fully exposed alpine ground with no shelter and long views out to the volcanoes. The moraine is loose and the glacier below it is heavily crevassed with big moats late in the season — rope up leaving camp, not after.

bivy.name: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
bivy.capacity: three at a squeeze
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp — a small stair-stepped shelf on the descent ridge overlooking the precipitous east face, where a party spent an unplanned full night out. No water, no shelter, cold, and highly exposed. On a peak this far in, a benightment is a realistic outcome rather than a remote one, so it is worth knowing this ledge is there and worth carrying enough to survive it.
